parts.partTitle: Cracking Open the JVM Class Object

beats.headline: How do frameworks inspect your code without importing it?
beats.subline: It isn't magic—it's the Java Reflection API.
beats.narration: Spring and Hibernate weren't compiled with your classes in mind. They use the Reflection API to inspect your types at runtime. But how does the JVM actually expose your code to them?

beats.title: The Runtime Mirror
beats.subtitle: From disk to heap-resident metadata
beats.narration: When a class is loaded, the JVM creates a java.lang.Class instance on the heap. This object is your entry point to every field, method, and annotation inside that class, regardless of visibility.

beats.title: Three Ways to Get a Class
beats.narration: You can grab a class literal, use an instance, or load by name. Pro tip: use the three-argument Class.forName to inspect metadata without triggering static initialization side effects.

beats.title: Member Visibility Traps
beats.narration: Mixing these up is a classic bug. getMethods only sees public stuff, including inherited ones. getDeclaredMethods sees everything, but only on the current class. You must walk the superclass chain manually.

beats.title: Reflection Basics Locked
takeaways: Use lazy loading to avoid static blocks
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Dynamic invocation and breaking JPMS encapsulation →
beats.narration: You've got the lookup down. In Part 2, we'll invoke methods dynamically and see how to bypass JPMS module restrictions.

beats.headline: Can you call a private method from another package?
beats.subline: Yes, but the JVM has some strong opinions about it.
beats.narration: Reflection lets you reach into private fields and methods. But since Java 9, the module system has been locking things down. Let's see how to invoke methods and handle the security wall.

beats.title: Dynamic Invocation
beats.narration: Method lookup requires exact parameter types. When invoking, pass null for static methods. Crucially, always unwrap InvocationTargetException; otherwise, you'll lose the real stack trace of your logic error.

beats.title: Bypassing JPMS
beats.caption: The --add-opens flag
beats.narration: Java 17+ strongly encapsulates internal packages. If you need to reflect into them, you must explicitly open the package at startup. In code, prefer trySetAccessible to avoid throwing exceptions.

beats.title: Reflection vs. MethodHandles
beats.narration: Reflection is slow because of boxing and repeated access checks. MethodHandles are the modern alternative—they're type-safe and JIT-inlinable, making them the standard for high-performance frameworks.

beats.title: Invocation & Handles
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Building custom annotations and meta-data traps →
beats.narration: Reflection is powerful, but use it sparingly. In Part 3, we'll build custom annotations and see why your runtime lookups might be returning null.

beats.headline: Why is your annotation returning null at runtime?
beats.subline: You missed the retention policy, and the JVM threw it away.
beats.narration: You defined an annotation, placed it on a method, and used reflection to find it. But it's null. It's not a bug in your code, it's a configuration trap in the annotation definition.

beats.title: Defining Runtime Annotations
beats.narration: The default retention is CLASS, which means the JVM discards it at runtime. You must explicitly set it to RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME if you want to read it via reflection.

beats.title: Retention Policies
beats.subtitle: Where does your metadata go?
beats.narration: SOURCE is for build tools like Lombok. CLASS is for bytecode weavers. Only RUNTIME survives the JVM loading process. If you want to read it, you need RUNTIME.

beats.title: Reading Annotations
beats.narration: Reading is simple once the retention is set. Check presence first, then pull the instance. The annotation object acts like a proxy, giving you access to the values defined in the source.

beats.title: Annotations Mastered
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Compile-time processing vs. Runtime reflection →
beats.narration: Annotations are the glue of modern Java. In Part 4, we'll see why moving this logic to compile-time is the ultimate performance hack.

beats.headline: Why are modern frameworks moving away from reflection?
beats.subline: Reflection is flexible, but compile-time processing is faster.
beats.narration: Reflection is slow because it happens at runtime. Modern tools like Dagger and MapStruct do the work at compile-time. Let's compare the two approaches.

beats.title: Reflection vs. APT
beats.narration: Reflection is great for plugins, but it kills startup time. Annotation processors generate plain Java code, so the JVM sees standard method calls. It's faster, safer, and perfect for GraalVM.

beats.title: The APT Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Generating code during compilation
beats.narration: Annotation processors hook into javac. They read your metadata and write new source files before compilation finishes. The final bytecode is just standard Java, with no reflection needed.

beats.title: Performance Summary
beats.caption: Choose your tool wisely
beats.narration: Use reflection for dynamic plugins. Use MethodHandles for high-throughput logic. Use annotation processors for everything else. Your startup time will thank you.
